pieces.text: All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genes affect its observable traits, including its appearance, its behavior, and which diseases it may have.
Genes may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.

Genes may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.

For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers.
Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.

contents.text: An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.

An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.

header.text: Some traits, like flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles determine whether an organism is homozygous or heterozygous for the gene.

contents.text: An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype FF or ff is homozygous for the flower color gene.
An organism with two different alleles for a gene is heterozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype Ff is heterozygous for the flower color gene.

header.text: The types of alleles in an organism's genotype determine the organism's phenotype. Some alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of a trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.

contents.text: A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant over the f allele. A pea plant with at least one F allele will have the F allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype FF or Ff will have purple flowers.

A recessive allele causes its version of the trait to appear only when the organism does not have any dominant alleles for the gene. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive to the F allele. A pea plant with only f alleles will have the f allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype ff will have white flowers.

subpoints.text: Some traits, such as flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles determine an organism's phenotype for the trait.

header.text: Some of the alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of the trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.

contents.text: A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant over the f allele. A pea plant with at least one F allele will have the F allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype FF or Ff will have purple flowers.

A recessive allele causes its version of the trait to appear only when the organism does not have any dominant alleles for the gene. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive to the F allele. A pea plant with only f alleles will have the f allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype ff will have white flowers.

pieces.text: To determine how many boxes in the Punnett square represent offspring with a hairy body or a hairless body, consider whether each phenotype is the dominant or recessive allele's version of the body hair trait.
The question tells you that the b allele, which is for a hairless body, is recessive to the B allele, which is for a hairy body.
A hairy body is the dominant allele's version of the body hair trait.
A cat with the dominant version of the body hair trait must have at least one dominant allele for the body hair gene.
The dominant allele for the body hair gene is B.
So, offspring with a hairy body must have the genotype BB or Bb.

A cat with the recessive version of the body hair trait must have only recessive alleles for the body hair gene.
The recessive allele for the body hair gene is b.
So, offspring with a hairless body must have the genotype bb.

subpoints.text: Some traits, such as flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles determine an organism's phenotype for the trait.

header.text: Some of the alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of the trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.

contents.text: A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant over the f allele. A pea plant with at least one F allele will have the F allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype FF or Ff will have purple flowers.

A recessive allele causes its version of the trait to appear only when the organism does not have any dominant alleles for the gene. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive to the F allele. A pea plant with only f alleles will have the f allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype ff will have white flowers.

subpoints.text: All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genes affect its observable traits, including its appearance, its behavior, and which diseases it may have. Each gene may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.

header.text: For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers. Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.

contents.text: An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.

An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.

subpoints.text: An organism's genotype depends on the genotypes of its parents. You can use the genotypes of two parents to predict the possible genotypes of their offspring with the help of a Punnett square.

The genotypes of the parents are shown on the top and left side of the Punnett square. The possible genotypes of the offspring are shown in the boxes inside the Punnett square.

contents.text: The following passage describes the effects of a gene mutation, which is a permanent change in a gene. Read the passage and then follow the instructions below.

elements.text: In plants such as the European cantaloupe, fruit ripening is affected by a substance called ethylene (ETH-uh-leen). Ethylene is made inside a plant's cells with the help of a protein called CmACO1. The CmACO1 protein is encoded by the CmACO1 gene.

A certain European cantaloupe plant had a mutation in its CmACO1 gene. Compared to the CmACO1 gene without a mutation, the mutated CmACO1 gene encoded a form of the CmACO1 protein with a different structure.

This different form of the CmACO1 protein could make only a small amount of ethylene. The fruits of this plant took longer to ripen than fruits from plants containing more ethylene. Farmers found this mutation useful because the fruit stayed good for a longer period of time after harvest.

elements.text: Common carp are a type of fish that have scales on their bodies. The pattern of scales on a common carp is established while the fish is developing inside its egg. During this time, a protein called Fgfr1a1 sends signals to the fish's body that direct the shape and spacing of the fish's scales. The signals from the Fgfr1a1 protein result in common carp with small, evenly spaced scales.
The Fgfr1a1 protein is encoded by the fgfr1a1 gene.

This different form of the Fgfr1a1 protein could not send signals to the fish's body.

elements.text: Cholesterol (koh-LES-ter-ol) is a fat-like substance that has many functions in the body. Cholesterol moves through the body in the blood. The amount of cholesterol in the blood is controlled by proteins, including the PCSK9 protein. The PCSK9 protein is encoded by the PCSK9 gene.
The PCSK9 protein adds cholesterol to the blood. The action of the PCSK9 protein can lead to blood cholesterol levels that may, over time, cause heart disease.
A certain person had a mutation in the PCSK9 gene. Compared to the PCSK9 gene without a mutation, the mutated PCSK9 gene encoded a form of the PCSK9 protein with a different structure.

This different form of the PCSK9 protein could add only a small amount of cholesterol to the blood. So, this person had a lower risk of developing heart disease than a person with more cholesterol in their blood.

elements.text: Muscle movement is controlled by charged atoms called ions. Ions move in and out of muscle cells through tube-like structures called channels.

elements.text: The eyes of fruit flies look red because they contain molecules called pigments, which color the eyes red. Cells in the eyes of fruit flies have parts that make these pigments from other molecules.
The molecules that will become pigments are brought inside these cell parts by a protein called a transporter. This transporter protein is encoded by the w gene.

Scientists in a lab found a fruit fly that had white eyes. This fly had a mutation in its w gene. Compared to the w gene without a mutation, the mutated w gene encoded a form of the transporter protein with a different structure.
This different form of the transporter protein could not bring molecules into the parts of the fly's eye cells where pigments are made. So, the fly's eyes had no pigments.

header.text: Genes and the environment affect an organism's growth and development in different ways:

contents.text: Genes contain information that cells use as instructions. These instructions tell cells how to build an organism's parts and how to carry out other biological processes. Different types of organisms have different sets of genes.

The environment provides the raw materials that an organism uses to grow and carry out biological processes. These raw materials include food, water, and other nutrients. The environment also includes conditions such as wind or high temperatures that can influence an organism's size and shape.
